title: Modi Convenes Economic War Room as West Asia Crisis Tests India's 7.7% Growth Story
excerpt: The PM-Economic Advisory Council meeting reviewed energy shock preparedness, trade route disruptions and reform blueprints — a day after GDP data confirmed India as the world's fastest-growing major economy
body:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday chaired a meeting of the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister (EAC-PM), convening what amounted to an economic war room as the West Asia conflict continues to rattle energy markets, trade flows and investor sentiment worldwide.

The meeting came barely 24 hours after India's GDP data for FY26 landed — confirming full-year growth of 7.7 per cent, with the January-March quarter clocking a robust 7.8 per cent. That performance makes India comfortably the fastest-growing major economy on the planet, but the EAC-PM's agenda made clear that sustaining the run is now the harder task.

## The Shadow of Hormuz

https://x.com/PMOIndia/status/2063140992300298654

At the centre of the discussion: the West Asia crisis and its ripple effects across India's economic landscape. The Strait of Hormuz — which carried roughly a fifth of global oil supply before it was effectively shuttered — has been a persistent source of anxiety since late February. With Brent crude flirting with $95 a barrel and having briefly touched $99 mid-week, India's energy import bill is becoming a structural headwind.

Members of the EAC-PM examined the conflict's implications for energy markets, trade routes and broader economic stability. The council's discussions reportedly went beyond the immediate oil shock, extending to second-order effects: the widening current account deficit, the pressure on the rupee (which weakened to 95.64 against the dollar earlier this week), and the risk of imported inflation feeding through to consumer prices.

## Reforms, Not Just Resilience

But the EAC-PM meeting was not purely defensive. Officials said a substantial portion of the deliberations focused on reforms to improve ease of living and ease of doing business — a policy frame the Modi government has leaned on heavily in its third term. The discussions covered governance efficiency, compliance reduction and measures to create a more attractive environment for investment and entrepreneurship.

"Chaired a meeting of the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister," Modi said in a social media post afterwards. "Deliberated on a wide range of issues relating to India's economic transformation and long-term development priorities. Also shared perspectives on adding more momentum to the reforms journey."

The meeting was attended by Principal Secretaries PK Mishra and Shaktikanta Das, alongside EAC-PM Chairman S Mahendra Dev and members including Sanjeev Sanyal, Shamika Ravi, Neelkanth Mishra and Nilesh Shah — a roster that blends academic economics with market-facing expertise.

## The Austerity Signal

The meeting's context extends beyond the conference room. In May, Modi had made an unusual public appeal asking citizens to reduce reliance on imported fuel, avoid international travel for a year, embrace work-from-home arrangements, carpool, shift to electric vehicles and promote Swadeshi goods. He even called for reduced gold purchases and lower edible oil consumption — a remarkable shopping list of behavioural nudges for a wartime economy that is not, technically, at war.

That austerity appeal, paired with Saturday's EAC-PM session, suggests the government is war-gaming scenarios where the Hormuz chokepoint remains closed well into the summer — precisely when fuel demand peaks globally.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs watching from abroad, the signal is mixed but instructive. India's growth story remains intact: 7.7 per cent in a year when most advanced economies are struggling to hold 2 per cent. The RBI held rates steady at 5.25 per cent on Friday, preserving its monetary policy ammunition for a potential external shock rather than front-loading stimulus.

But the vulnerability is real. India imports over 85 per cent of its crude oil, and with Russian crude now commanding a premium (rather than the discount that prevailed through 2023-24), the energy bill arithmetic is tightening. The capital gains tax exemption on foreign bond investments announced earlier this week was a signal that New Delhi is actively working to attract dollars — and shore up the rupee — through every available channel.

The EAC-PM's next move, and whether Saturday's deliberations translate into specific policy action, will determine how India navigates what could be the most challenging external environment of the Modi era.
